learn.title: Small quantities: a little, a few, very little, very few, less, fewer
learn.html:
To talk about small quantities, English distinguishes between uncountable nouns (things you cannot count: milk, rice, butter, food) and plural countable nouns (eggs, carrots, calories). In Spanish we use «poco/a/os/as» for everything; in English you have to choose.

MeaningUncountableCountable (plural)
some, a little (enough)a little buttera few slices of cheese
almost none, not muchvery little foodvery few frozen meals
less (comparison)less fatfewer calories
in negativesnot much foodnot many vegetables
  • A little / a few sound positive: We have a few eggs (we can cook something).
  • Very little / very few sound negative: We have very few eggs (there are almost none).
  • Much and many are mainly used in questions and negatives: There isn't much juice. Are there many apples?
  • Measures (a carton of, a kilo of) let you count uncountable things: two cartons of juice.

watch.why: Meat is uncountable: little, not few.
Vegetables is countable in the plural: many.

watch.wrong: Fruit has less calories than cake.
watch.right: Fruit has fewer calories than cake.
watch.why: Calories are counted: fewer, not less.

watch.wrong: We have a few of milk.
watch.why: Milk is uncountable; also, a little doesn't take of.

learn.title: too, too much, too many and enough
learn.html:
These words tell you whether something is «more than necessary» (too) or whether it is enough (enough). Their position changes.

WordUseExample
too much + uncountablemore than neededI ate too much food.
too many + plural countablemore than neededI ate too many fries.
too + adjective / adverbmore than neededHe's too full. She eats too slowly.
verb + too muchtoo much (action)She talks too much.
enough + nounsufficientI didn't eat enough food.
adjective / adverb + enoughsufficientlyThe salad wasn't filling enough. She doesn't eat fast enough.
  • Too much / too many / enough also work alone: I ate too much. I didn't eat enough.
  • Enough goes before the noun but after the adjective or adverb: enough money but rich enough.
  • Too has a negative meaning («more than is good»). To say «very» in a positive way, use very: very good, not too good.

watch.why: With a verb you need an adverb: too slowly.
Too means excessive, negative; to praise, use very.

learn.title: Giving examples: like, for example, such as
learn.html:
In a text or conversation you can illustrate an idea with examples. There are three common ways, with different punctuation.

ExpressionHow it is usedExample
likeinside the sentence; informalTry some tropical fruit, like mango or pineapple.
such asinside the sentence; a little more formalYou can add toppings, such as coconut or chocolate.
for examplenew sentence (or between commas); followed by a complete exampleThere are many snacks. For example, people eat roasted corn.
  • There is no such like or for example as.
  • After like and such as usually comes just a noun (or several): fruits such as mangoes and oranges.

watch.wrong: She eats foods such like broccoli.
watch.right: She eats foods such as broccoli.
watch.why: The expression is such as, not such like.

watch.wrong: I like snacks, for example as chips.
watch.right: I like snacks, for example chips.
watch.why: For example doesn't combine with as.
After For example at the start, use a comma.

learn.title: Letting someone else decide and politely turning down offers
learn.html:
Letting someone else decide:

  • Either one (is fine). / Either way (is fine). — either one is fine.
  • Whatever you're having. / Whatever you prefer. — whatever you want / whatever you choose.
  • Whichever is easier (for you). — whichever is easier for you.

Politely turning down food or drink offers:

  • No, thanks. Maybe later. — not now; maybe later.
  • I'm fine. Really. — I'm fine, really.
  • I'm OK for now. But thanks. — I'm fine for now, but thanks.

Example: A: Do you want tea or coffee? B: Either one is fine. Whatever you're having.

write.model:
I think I eat too much sugar. I drink two or three sodas a day, and I have too many cookies after dinner. I also eat too much bread, because it is cheap and easy. On the other hand, I don't eat enough vegetables or fruit. I only have a few vegetables on my plate, usually some lettuce and tomato.

I want to eat less fried food and fewer sweets this year. I would like to drink less soda and have fewer snacks between meals. Fortunately, healthy food is easy to buy. For example, I always buy a kilo of apples and a bag of carrots every week. I also buy a carton of milk and a jar of honey for breakfast, and a can of beans for lunch.

I prefer grilled chicken to fried chicken, and I like steamed vegetables like broccoli and carrots. I also enjoy baked fish, such as salmon, but it is expensive. Right now, I'm trying to eat enough protein, and I drink more water, so I feel much better.

Between 120 and 160 words
write.model:
Hi Daniel,

I'm so happy that you're coming to dinner on Saturday! What do you want to eat? I can make pasta or chicken with rice. Do you want something to drink, like juice or water? If you can't decide, I'll choose for you. Either one is fine with me, so please tell me what you prefer.

I went to the supermarket yesterday. I have a little cheese, a few tomatoes and some onions. I have very little milk, so I need to buy more. There are very few eggs left, too. For dessert, I have some fruit, such as mangoes and bananas.

You asked if you can bring something. Thanks, but I'm OK for now! I have everything I need. If you want to help, you can come early and talk to me while I cook.

See you on Saturday!
Marta

reading.title: Eating better, one step at a time
reading.intro: Read the text about Daniela and answer.
paragraphs: Daniela is thirty-two and works in an office in Guadalajara. Three months ago her doctor told her, "You're eating too much fast food and you don't sleep enough." Daniela was surprised, but she decided to change her habits slowly.

First, she looked in her kitchen. In the freezer there were too many frozen dinners, and in the cabinet there were two boxes of cookies and a big bag of potato chips. In the fridge, however, there was very little fresh fruit and only a few vegetables. "I buy too many treats," she said, "and I never have enough time to cook."

Now she goes to the local market every Saturday. She buys a kilo of tomatoes, a pound of green peppers, a few carrots and some broccoli. She also buys a liter of water and a carton of eggs. At first, the vegetables were more expensive than the frozen meals, but she says that fresh food has more flavor and fewer calories.

Daniela doesn't cook anything difficult. She prefers simple recipes: steamed vegetables, grilled chicken, boiled eggs and baked potatoes. She doesn't fry food very often now. "Fried food is delicious, but it has too much fat," she explains. On Sundays, she makes a big pot of soup and puts a few portions in the freezer for the week.

She isn't perfect, and she doesn't want to be. She still eats a slice of cake or a few tacos with her friends on weekends. "Treats are fine, as long as you don't eat too many," she says. After three months, Daniela has lost four kilos, she sleeps better, and her mood is better, too. "Healthy food isn't boring," she says. "You just need good ingredients, a little time and enough patience."

Her friend Carlos was not sure at first. "Salads are boring," he said. But last month Daniela invited him for dinner. She cooked grilled shrimp with pineapple, steamed rice and a green salad, and she made a simple dessert with mango. Carlos ate two plates and asked for the recipe. Now he goes to the market with her on Saturdays, and he says that cooking at home is not too difficult.
